content:
Earlier this year, I replaced a battery-powered push mower with an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. You can manually drive it around the yard to create a virtual map, and once set up, it will automatically handle the mowing according to a schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe it may be an easier-to-use option for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 that I reviewed earlier this year lies in how the two machines understand your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. It has three built-in cameras that allow the mower to automatically map your lawn, without the need to install underground boundary wires, nor an independent RTK antenna.

Automatic mapping takes longer to create the initial map. But I think it may be easier for people who are less tech-savvy and do not enjoy "learning by doing."

To test this idea, I asked my mother, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any assistance from me. She said everything worked well. However, I'm not sure whether she had the patience to first manually remote-control the robot along the entire boundary and then mark out each area to be avoided one by one.

The automatic mapping caused a small problem in my front yard. Since there is no fence or physical divider between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I marked that area as a no-go zone in the app to correct it. This shows that if there is no clear visual boundary between lawns, you may need to pay special attention during the initial mapping.

A look through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to keep the view open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the back garden.

This feature isn't necessary for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and occasionally helps explain why it slows down or avoids certain obstacles. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view feature.

The two iPhone apps share many things in common in other respects. Both let you schedule jobs, adjust mowing settings, create zones, mark no-go areas, and remote-control the mower.

TerraMow has a particularly clever design for that last feature. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the primary use of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a schedule without any intervention. However, TerraMow's joystick control is well suited for tidying up missed spots.

At times, I almost felt like I was controlling the robot with my mind (it was quite a pleasant feeling). I could walk next to the mower holding my iPhone, looking down, and with just slight movements of my thumb, the robot would follow my directions.

Every robotic mower app should imitate this type of control.

More aggressive mowing performance

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. In my testing, it cut lower and was also louder during operation.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is noisy, but the difference between the two is quite noticeable. The Anthbot operates extremely quietly, making it easy to forget that it's working—even when it's mowing at night with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. This makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective cover in the box to shield the charging base, whereas Anthbot's protective cover must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performs reliably. I relied on it for several consecutive weeks without having to personally take over the daily mowing.

When automatic map adjustments become too "smart"

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you temporarily cannot perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I encountered an interesting edge case. Parts of the yard were waterlogged, and the TerraMow sensibly avoided those areas on its next run.

Within those skipped circles, the grass subsequently grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret this growth as an area to continue avoiding, leaving it uncut even after the ground had dried.

I eventually used the app's remote-control function to manually drive the mower through that patch of taller grass. Once the area returned to normal lawn condition, automatic mowing resumed working normally.

Regularly trimming the edges also helps the TerraMow reach the boundaries smoothly. Tall grass growing along an unclear dividing line might otherwise be misidentified as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

In comparison, Anthbot's approach involves less automatic adjustment. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles you set. This requires more work upfront, but it also avoids situations where the map "changes its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

After trying out both systems, for most people I would lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera approach.

Burying boundary wires is completely out of the question for me, and installing an RTK base station means I have to set up, maintain, and look after one more piece of hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property boundary needs manual correction, and its automatic adjustment behaviour once mistook tall weeds for permanent obstacles.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, fun real-time camera views, and the best robotic mower app manual control experience I have used.

I do enjoy gardening, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this job over to a robot frees up more time for landscaping, trimming, and detail work, while keeping the lawn neat and attractive.

The TerraMow V1000 is fully capable of handling this job, and I would recommend it—especially for those who want to skip burying wires, installing an RTK antenna, or walking around the entire yard holding an iPhone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently priced at US$999 on Amazon, and can be purchased on the website using a US$200 coupon. You can also buy it from the official TerraMow website.
